item.title: Amupitan’s resignation report false, misleading — INEC
item.description: By Ayobami Okerinde The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has refuted a social media report suggesting that its Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, is set to resign. The commission described the claim, which was shared alongside an image online, as fabricated and misleading. INEC made its position known on Saturday through a statement on its official X account, urging Nigerians to disregard the report and refrain from circulating unverified information. “The claim is FALSE, FABRICATED AND MISLEADING,” the commission stated. “Members of the public are urged to disregard the fabricated report, refrain from sharing unverified information and rely solely on INEC’s official communication channels for authentic information. “Stop the spread of fake news.” Recall Vanguard reported that Amupitan was confronted by protesters outside Chatham House on Thursday, calling for his resignation over alleged shortcomings in the voters’ register. The protesters surrounded his vehicle as he departed a discussion on Nigeria’s preparations for the 2027 elections, with some demanding that he step out to address their concerns. The post Amupitan’s resignation report false, misleading — INEC appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
item.description: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice. The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars. The missing ice Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets. Read full article Comments

item.title: COP31: Democrats Pledge Climate Actions Despite Trump Absence
item.description: Fresh from their US midterm election triumph, an emboldened group of Democratic lawmakers descended on the COP31 climate talks shunned by President Donald Trump on Saturday to signal their commitment to tackling global warming. The 18-strong delegation joined the annual UN conference in Turkey after their party regained control of both chambers of Congress in a landslide victory last week cheered by climate campaigners. “Many of our allies and partners across the world think the United States has not been predictable or dependable. So we have a lot of trust to earn back,” Florida Representative Kathy Castor told AFP. “We have so much work to do. And yes, I hope the United States gets back on track with urgent climate action,” she said after the group took photos in front of a large COP31 sign in a sprawling expo centre. Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham delivers a speech during the High-Level Segment for Heads of States and Government at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) at the Antalya Expo Center in Antalya on November 12, 2026. (Photo by Stefan Rousseau / POOL / AFP) | Stefan Rousseau / POOL / AFP The election has been a topic of discussion at COP31 in Antalya, with hopes that Democrats can restore some clean energy policies and that a pro-climate president can be elected in two years. “What happened in the US is remarkable, and a much needed shift that we all needed, not only from a climate perspective, but overall,” Harjeet Singh, strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, told AFP. Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has rolled back some of the clean energy policies of his predecessors, promoted oil drilling, pulled the United States out of the Paris Agreement and kept his country out of the UN’s climate negotiations. “It is absolutely shameful that the Trump administration operates this way, that this is an administration that is filled with climate deniers, that is beholden to big oil in the United States,” Yassamin Ansari, an Arizona lawmaker, told AFP. Swedish activist Greta Thunberg arrives at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, on November 10, 2026. Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall slightly in 2026 due to the expansion of renewable energy and the oil price shock sparked by the Iran war, researchers said Tuesday. ‘Climate Action Alive In America’ Ansari and other members of the delegation spoke at a panel focused on the midterm elections, attracting a crowd that overflowed outside the “America Is All In” pavilion. Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has rolled back some of the clean energy policies of his predecessors, promoted oil drilling, pulled the United States out of the Paris Agreement and kept his country out of the UN’s climate negotiations. “It is absolutely shameful that the Trump administration operates this way, that this is an administration that is filled with climate deniers, that is beholden to big oil in the United States,” Yassamin Ansari, an Arizona lawmaker, told AFP. Swedish activist Greta Thunberg arrives at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, on November 10, 2026. Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall slightly in 2026 due to the expansion of renewable energy and the oil price shock sparked by the Iran war, researchers said Tuesday. ‘Climate Action Alive In America’ Ansari and other members of the delegation spoke at a panel focused on the midterm elections, attracting a crowd that overflowed outside the “America Is All In” pavilion. The group reminded COP31 delegates that, while Trump has rejected clean energy, US states and local governments have continued to promote renewables and other pro-climate policies. A group of US mayors and governors visited COP31 earlier this week, along with former US vice president Al Gore and former US climate envoy and secretary of state John Kerry. “Despite the setbacks that we’re experiencing through this Trump administration, climate action is alive in America,” California Congressman Raul Ruiz told the panel. The president’s Republican party was handed a resounding defeat last week in large part due to anger over soaring energy prices and Trump’s costly war with Iran. Democrats have vowed to use their majority in the House and the Senate to launch investigations into the administration’s climate policies and propose clean energy legislation. But Trump still has two years left in office and has vowed to wield his veto power. “At a time where Americans from all political backgrounds want to see their energy bills reduced, this administration will be very hard pressed to veto legislation that will bring down costs for the American people,” Ansari said. item.title: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
item.description: More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape , one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine , but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall. Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production. As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management. Read full article Comments

item.title: Rings of Power Just Changed the Nazgul in 1 Terrifying Way: ‘They Still Have a Human Side’
item.description: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 sees Sauron begin to recruit the nine lieutenants that will one day become the Nazgûl, or Ringraiths. While details in J.R.R. Tolkien’s lore are a bit scarce when it comes to the gradual transformation of the Ringwraiths, Rings of Power initially presents the rings as miraculous gifts that transform the Men who wear them into Nazgnagôl, or "Ring-servants.” Rather than immediately enslaving their wearers, Sauron's rings heal their injuries, cure terrible afflictions, and grant them extraordinary power. The catch is that every gift brings its recipient closer to surrendering his freedom.

item.title: NAFDAC uncovers unregistered cosmetics, falsified medicines, banned soaps at Trade Fair Complex
item.description: By Chioma Obinna The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, NAFDAC, has uncovered a suspected illegal cosmetics production and packaging operation at the Tools and Hardware section of Trade Fair Complex, Lagos. The raid exposes a network of unregistered products and materials allegedly intended for illicit manufacturing. Read Also: NAFDAC uncovers another fake herbal factory in Lagos, arrests manager The discovery followed an enforcement operation at the sprawling market along the Lagos-Badagry Expressway. Officials found unlabelled cosmetics, empty product containers, packaging materials and already-produced creams across different floors of a two-storey building. In a video of the operation shared on the Agency’s official X account on Saturday, Mr. Olakunle Ojo, NAFDAC enforcement team lead, and other officials were seen inspecting the building and displaying the recovered materials, raising concerns over the production and circulation of cosmetics of unknown origin and regulatory status. “This is exactly what we are able to find at this particular location,” Mr. Ojo said while displaying various packaging materials and empty containers. The inspection revealed packaging materials bearing names such as turmeric vitamin C and other cosmetic product descriptions, alongside empty shampoo tubes, lotion containers and materials suspected to be intended for the packaging of unregistered products. On the upper floors, officials discovered additional packaging materials, including containers for different cosmetic products, as well as already-produced glutawide cream. The agency also displayed materials bearing different product names, but could not immediately establish the identity and regulatory status of some of the substances and products found at the premises. NAFDAC described the operation as part of its ongoing enforcement activities at the Trade Fair Complex, where it has uncovered several suspected illegal manufacturing, storage and distribution activities. ‘Drugs’ In a related discovery at the complex, the agency uncovered a warehouse on the last floor of a building containing packaging materials for suspected falsified medicines, including Augmentin 625mg and Amplicloxa. Bottle caps bearing the Gordon’s Gin brand were also reportedly found among the materials. The latest discoveries add to a series of enforcement operations by NAFDAC at the Trade Fair market. In previous raids, the agency recovered 728 cartons of Crusader soap, 718 cartons of E45 soap and quantities of Extract Gold whitening soap, products it said were banned by the Federal Government. The repeated discoveries have raised concerns about the scale of illegal product manufacturing and repackaging activities operating within the market, as well as the potential risks to unsuspecting consumers. Vanguard News The post NAFDAC uncovers unregistered cosmetics, falsified medicines, banned soaps at Trade Fair Complex appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: NYSC, Army Strengthen Security Collaboration In Taraba
item.description: The National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) is seeking strengthened collaboration with the 10 Division, Nigeria Army, to enhance the safety and security of corps members in Taraba State. The NYSC is also commending the Nigeria Army for its sustained efforts in combating terrorism and other forms of criminality in the state. The Area Director, NYSC North East Area Office 2, Odoba Oche, stated this during a courtesy call to the General Officer Commanding 10 Division and Commander, Operation Mountain Watch, Major General Nnebeife, at headquarters 10 Division, Jalingo, Taraba State Capital. Oche, who oversees NYSC activities in Adamawa, Gombe and Taraba states, praised the Nigeria Army for unalloyed protection of orientation camps. NYSC, Army Strengthen Security Collaborations In Taraba. For Major General Nnebeife, the General Officer Commanding 10 Division, Nigeria Army, the NYSC is a critical partner in promoting National Unity and integration. According to him, both the Nigeria Army and the NYSC share a common commitment to patriotism, national cohesion and service to the nation, and fostering unity among Nigerians. The GOC assured the Area Director of the Nigeria Army’s commitment to protecting lives and property, particularly the safety of corps members during orientation exercises and movement to places of primary assignments. The post NYSC, Army Strengthen Security Collaboration In Taraba appeared first on Channels Television .

item.title: Nollywood sequel “Issakaba: The Return” hits cinemas after 25 years
item.description: Nollywood action thriller ‘Issakaba: The Return’ has returned to cinemas nationwide after 25 years of the release of the original movie, ‘Issakaba’. The director, Lancelot Imasuen, announced the cinema release in a post on his Instagram page on Friday, expressing excitement over the return of the popular movie franchise to the big screen. In the post, Imasuen described the production as the return of a legend and urged movie lovers to watch the film in cinemas. The sequel features veteran actor Sam Dede reprising his role as Ebube, leader of the Issakaba Boys, while introducing other actors from different generations of Nollywood. Other cast members include Chidi Mokeme, Iyabo Ojo, Regina Daniels, Chiwetalu Agu, Alex Osifo, Charles Okafor, Nosa Rex and Mark Angel. Directed by Imasuen, who also helmed the original production, ‘Issakaba: The Return’ revisits the story of the fictional vigilante group against the backdrop of contemporary Nigerian society. The original film, released in 2001, drew inspiration from the activities of the Bakassi Boys, a vigilante group that emerged in south-eastern Nigeria to combat criminal activities. The sequel, distributed by Blue Pictures, brings together returning actors and newer Nollywood performers, marking the revival of one of the industry’s recognised action film franchises. (NAN) The post Nollywood sequel “Issakaba: The Return” hits cinemas after 25 years appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
item.description: null Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. How to measure distances in the night sky using your outstretched hand. (Image credit: Created in Canva Pro) Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA . Interested in seeing and capturing the planets for yourself? Then be sure to read our guide on everything you need to observe and photograph the planets of the solar system, along with our picks of the top telescopes , cameras and lenses for exploring the night sky in 2026. Editor's Note: If you would like to share your photos of Mars and Jupiter with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

item.title: 2027: Alake, Akpabio, Others Await Tinubu’s Arrival In Jos For Presidential Campaign [PHOTOS]
item.description: Minister of Solid Minerals, Dele Alake; the Senate President, Godswill Akpabio; Deputy Senate President, Barau Jibrin, Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, are among several dignitaries gathered at the arrival wing of the Yakubu Gowon Airport in Jos, Plateau State, awaiting the arrival of President Bola Tinubu. The President is expected in Jos ahead of the APC North-Central Presidential Rally, which is part of the party’s activities towards the 2027 general elections. Other party leaders, government officials, and stakeholders are also at the airport to receive the President. Sen. Ned Nwoko, Solid Minerals Minister, Dele Alake, and others are expecting the arrival of President Tinubu at the airport as he takes a 2027 campaign rally to Jos on Saturday, November 14, 2026. The Plateau State Police Command said it has deployed adequate security personnel across Jos and intensified surveillance ahead of President Bola Tinubu’s presidential campaign visit to the state on Saturday. Solid Minerals Minister, Dele Alake, Information Minister, Mohammed Idris and others awaiting arrival of President Tinubu in Jos, on November 14, 2026. Supporters of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Plateau State are trooping into the Zaria Road Stadium in Jos ahead of the arrival of President Tinubu. APC Supporters gather in Jos ahead of Tinubu’s presidential campaign, on Saturday, November 14, 2026 The party’s National Chairman, Professor Nentawe Yilwatda, alongside other top national and state party officials, is also expected at the venue for the rally, which will bring together Governor Caleb Mutfwang, party leaders, stakeholders and supporters from across the North Central region. APC Supporters gather in Jos ahead of Tinubu’s presidential campaign. The atmosphere at the stadium is building up as supporters arrive, while preparations continue ahead of the President’s visit. Deployed police officers in Jos on Saturday, November 14, 2026. The Deputy Inspector-General of Police in charge of the North Central Zone, DIG Isyaku Mohammad, disclosed this while addressing journalists in Jos, assuring residents that comprehensive security arrangements had been put in place to ensure a peaceful visit. DIG Mohammad, who is coordinating security operations for the presidential visit, said the Police had conducted security assessments covering the airport, routes to the campaign venue and the venue itself. He added that uniformed and plainclothes officers had been deployed, while patrols and stop-and-search operations had been intensified across the city. The post 2027: Alake, Akpabio, Others Await Tinubu’s Arrival In Jos For Presidential Campaign [PHOTOS] appeared first on Channels Television .

item.title: Triumphant Democrats descend on COP31 snubbed by Trump
item.description: Fresh from their US midterm election triumph, an emboldened group of Democratic lawmakers descended on the COP31 climate talks shunned by President Donald Trump on Saturday to signal their commitment to tackling global warming. The 18-strong delegation joined the annual UN conference in Turkey after their party regained control of both chambers of Congress in a landslide victory last week cheered by climate campaigners. “Many of our allies and partners across the world think the United States has not been predictable or dependable. So we have a lot of trust to earn back,” Florida Representative Kathy Castor told AFP. “We have so much work to do. And yes, I hope the United States gets back on track with urgent climate action,” she said after the group took photos in front of a large COP31 sign in a sprawling expo centre. The election has been a topic of discussion at COP31 in Antalya, with hopes that Democrats can restore some clean energy policies and that a pro-climate president can be elected in two years. “What happened in the US is remarkable, and a much needed shift that we all needed, not only from a climate perspective, but overall,” Harjeet Singh, strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, told AFP. Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has rolled back some of the clean energy policies of his predecessors, promoted oil drilling, pulled the United States out of the Paris Agreement and kept his country out of the UN’s climate negotiations. “It is absolutely shameful that the Trump administration operates this way, that this is an administration that is filled with climate deniers, that is beholden to big oil in the United States,” Yassamin Ansari, an Arizona lawmaker, told AFP. – ‘Climate action alive in America’ – Ansari and other members of the delegation spoke at a panel focused on the midterm elections, attracting a crowd that overflowed outside the “America Is All In” pavilion. The group reminded COP31 delegates that, while Trump has rejected clean energy, US states and local governments have continued to promote renewables and other pro-climate policies. A group of US mayors and governors visited COP31 earlier this week, along with former US vice president Al Gore and former US climate envoy and secretary of state John Kerry. “Despite the setbacks that we’re experiencing through this Trump administration, climate action is alive in America,” California Congressman Raul Ruiz told the panel. The president’s Republican party was handed a resounding defeat last week in large part due to anger over soaring energy prices and Trump’s costly war with Iran. Democrats have vowed to use their majority in the House and the Senate to launch investigations into the administration’s climate policies and propose clean energy legislation. But Trump still has two years left in office and has vowed to wield his veto power. “At a time where Americans from all political backgrounds want to see their energy bills reduced, this administration will be very hard pressed to veto legislation that will bring down costs for the American people,” Ansari said. The post Triumphant Democrats descend on COP31 snubbed by Trump appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about
item.description: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. item.content:encoded: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register : "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure. "Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy." Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®

item.title: US nationwide flight ground stop: "Our routers got overloaded with data"
item.description: On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop. More than 8,200 flights, or over 31% of those scheduled in the United States, were canceled. The ground stop lasted nearly five hours and was the longest in the country since September 11, 2001. Officials blamed outdated air traffic communications equipment, and said that there was no evidence of a cyber attack. The airspace is now reopened and flights have resumed.

item.title: Airspace Now ‘Opened Up,’ No Cyberattack — US
item.description: The United States on Friday lifted an hours-long ground stop at the nation’s airports, with top officials explaining that the disruption was due to old equipment and not a cyberattack or sweeping Microsoft outage. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told a late-night briefing at the White House that US airspace was now “opened up,” while warning it would take time for the travel chaos to clear. “At 8:15 tonight Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Duffy said. “Now does that mean every flight is going to fly right now? It’s going to be slow.” Passengers wait for updates at a check-in area at Terminal 7 at Los Angeles International Airport, in Los Angeles on November 13, 2026. US aviation regulators issued an extremely rare ground stop of all flights across the country on November 13 after a major communications outage which the Department of Homeland Security said did not appear to be the result of any “nefarious attack.” The breakdown came a day after Duffy and the White House had formally asked Congress for $30 billion to upgrade and modernize the US Air Traffic Control System. “Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down,” Duffy said. “It’s the old hardware that went down, and I think the question for the American people is: Do you want your Congress to fund this?” Duffy, however, insisted it was still safe for Americans to fly. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin dismissed speculation about a coordinated cyber assault on the United States, or any link to the Microsoft outage that affected services worldwide. “Welcome to Friday the 13th, right? You know, I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft. I know a lot of people are making that jump,” Mullin said. Mullin added there was “actually no cyber attack.” “When we start looking at cyber threats, cyber attacks, typically some people are going to raise their hand up and say, ‘Hey, we did that.’ There’s no chatter.’ We haven’t seen any footprints,” he added. But he said US security and law enforcement agencies were still checking and had ruled nothing out. Passengers wait in line to retrieve their luggage as flights were cancelled at Chicago O’Hare International Airport in Chicago on November 13, 2026. The two officials also defended President Donald Trump, who had yet to comment on the air stoppage some five hours after it began. “President Trump immediately had people in his office,” Mullin said. “We were communicating.” Passengers wait at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Washington, DC on November 13, 2026. AFP The post Airspace Now ‘Opened Up,’ No Cyberattack — US appeared first on Channels Television .

item.title: 20 Years Ago, the Best Sci-Fi Show of the Century Delivered the Most Epic Space Battle in TV History
item.description: Two decades later, this spectacle from Battlestar Galactica season 3’s “Exodus, Part 2” remains unforgettable sci-fi TV. It’s dazzling and horrifying, and still one of the coolest things ever broadcast on science-fiction television. From a tactical standpoint, the “Adama Maneuver” is absolutely bonkers and one of the riskiest spaceship tactics, perhaps ever (sorry, Vice-Admiral Holdo). What if the ship had gotten torn apart from ripping through the atmosphere? What if the FTL drive malfunctioned or didn’t activate in time? Somehow, it’s also not even the most visually impressive sequence in the episode.

item.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
item.description: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. item.dc:creator: Connor Jones
item.content:encoded: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly. There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs. "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content." Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories. With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process. Success of user reports trails away As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially. Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent. Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures. The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly. Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests. Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report , it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny. Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment. The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force. England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference " to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves. Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms. She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.' "In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered. "So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

item.title: De la Fuente feels the strain as Lamine Yamal club v country debate rages in Spain
item.description: Head coach hits out at ‘lies’ as suggestions of preferential treatment for young star overshadow preparations for England game in Madrid From the London Palladium to Madrid’s Metropolitano, they’re all here. On Sunday night, the footballers who lifted the game’s biggest awards meet again three weeks later and on the field this time, dinner jackets but not a single man left behind. Harry Kane, the Ballon d’Or and Gerd Müller trophy winner. Unai Simón, holder of the Lev Yashin award . Luis de la Fuente , the coach of the year who on Thursday night announced that also joining them will be Lamine Yamal , the kid who lifted the Kopa award as the best young player for the third year running and said he would have preferred Pau Cubarsí to be standing there instead. And, yes, Cubarsí will be there too for the final Nations League group game. At 1.45pm the world and European champions landed back at Madrid’s Barajas airport from Prague, where they had won again, before making their way by bus to their Las Rozas HQ, around the M40 motorway to the north-west of the capital. At about the same time, Lamine Yamal arrived from Barcelona, due in at midday. As was Mikel Oyarzabal , scorer of the winner at Euro 2024 and Spain’s top marksman this summer (not that he would ever tell you so) from San Sebastián. At 7.30pm, they trained, preparing to meet the World Cup semi-finalists and the team they defeated in Berlin at the end of Euro 2024. Two starters from the World Cup final will be absent: Dani Olmo and the captain, 2024 Ballon d’Or winner Rodri , are injured. But everyone else will be there. Continue reading...

item.title: New Scientist readers on how the magazine has shaped their lives
item.description: Have you been reading New Scientist since the start? Getty Images/Westend61 The first issue of New Scientist was published on 22 November 1956, and some of our readers have been with us since the very beginning. We asked subscribers, young and old, to tell us how they first encountered the magazine and how New Scientist has influenced their lives. The volume of responses and the gratitude expressed within them were quite overwhelming. Here are some of our favourites, featuring a spectacular maggot experiment, science-inspired poetry and even a match made on the short-lived New Scientist dating site. Huge thanks to everyone who wrote in. I was interested to see that New Scientist was launched “for all those men and women who are interested in scientific discovery and in its industrial, commercial and social consequences”. At the age of 13, I saved up a shilling from my Saturday morning “jobs” to purchase the first edition on 22 November 1956 and became one of those people interested in scientific discovery. Seventy years later, I remain a subscriber, after a scientific career that took me to many (if not, most!) countries in the world. New Scientist covered things like the opening of Jodrell Bank telescope in 1957. Since that was only about 50 miles (80 kilometres) away, it necessitated a bike ride to see what it really looked like! Peter Hall Advertisement I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70! I do recall my encounter with the first edition: I was at Bec Grammar School in south London in a second-year physics class – it was 1956. The teacher, a genial boffin-type, announced the advent of the new publication and handed out copies – all I remember is its grey (or was it beige?) pages, which I read in a perfunctory way (I was only 12!) little thinking it would follow me through life and around the globe. Robyn Williams I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958. My science master at Malvern had recognised my interest in science and technology and he bought the very first issue of New Scientist with his own money. At the next science class, he stood up in front of the whole class and waved the first issue, saying, “Young Inman, a new UK science and technology magazine has been published and here is the first issue for you.” I went on to reach 60 years as a member of the UK Institution of Civil Engineers. Peter Inman 1956 puts me back at school – Fettes College in Edinburgh. The school adopted New Scientist from its first edition and it was available in the library, where senior boys interested in science were recommended to read it. And so began a lifetime of New Scientist – I have been a regular for as long as I can remember and a subscriber for a very long time. I am very grateful to New Scientist for maintaining my interest in all the sciences and new developments, which I am sure has helped me to think laterally and to have a greater understanding of what makes everything tick. Frank Eva

item.content:encoded: Have you been reading New Scientist since the start? Getty Images/Westend61 The first issue of New Scientist was published on 22 November 1956, and some of our readers have been with us since the very beginning. The volume of responses and the gratitude expressed within them were quite overwhelming. Here are some of our favourites, featuring a spectacular maggot experiment, science-inspired poetry and even a match made on the short-lived New Scientist dating site. Huge thanks to everyone who wrote in. At the age of 13, I saved up a shilling from my Saturday morning “jobs” to purchase the first edition on 22 November 1956 and became one of those people interested in scientific discovery. Seventy years later, I remain a subscriber, after a scientific career that took me to many (if not, most!) countries in the world. New Scientist covered things like the opening of Jodrell Bank telescope in 1957. Since that was only about 50 miles (80 kilometres) away, it necessitated a bike ride to see what it really looked like! Peter Hall Advertisement I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70! I do recall my encounter with the first edition: I was at Bec Grammar School in south London in a second-year physics class – it was 1956. The teacher, a genial boffin-type, announced the advent of the new publication and handed out copies – all I remember is its grey (or was it beige?) pages, which I read in a perfunctory way (I was only 12!) little thinking it would follow me through life and around the globe. Robyn Williams I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958. My science master at Malvern had recognised my interest in science and technology and he bought the very first issue of New Scientist with his own money. At the next science class, he stood up in front of the whole class and waved the first issue, saying, “Young Inman, a new UK science and technology magazine has been published and here is the first issue for you.” I went on to reach 60 years as a member of the UK Institution of Civil Engineers. Peter Inman 1956 puts me back at school – Fettes College in Edinburgh. The school adopted New Scientist from its first edition and it was available in the library, where senior boys interested in science were recommended to read it. And so began a lifetime of New Scientist – I have been a regular for as long as I can remember and a subscriber for a very long time. I am very grateful to New Scientist for maintaining my interest in all the sciences and new developments, which I am sure has helped me to think laterally and to have a greater understanding of what makes everything tick. Frank Evans As a pupil in the mid-1960s at a girls’ grammar school in the north of England, one day I picked up a copy of New Scientist in the library. I was mind-blown by an article about Albert Einstein’s theories of relativity and time dilation, including a coloured diagram! I went on to study physical and material sciences at university and worked for eight years in research. But motherhood and misogyny (in those days before equal opportunities legislation) led me to change tack and I’ve been making pottery by hand for over 55 years. I like to think my science education hasn’t been wasted, but handed down to my daughters, one of whom reads New Scientist online in France. Every week, the paper issue landing on my doormat is devoured with excitement! Anne Rodgers Read more Trustworthy science journalism is more essential than ever The stories that most interested me were about emerging electronics, the Sputnik satellite and the launch of Laika the space dog. The last of these prompted me to construct a module to house a maggot atop a 3-pence standard firework rocket and launch it. I later recovered the maggot unharmed and used it as fishing bait the next day. Mel We are a group of 12 ladies “of a certain age” who meet once a month to discuss three or four articles from New Scientist . We tackle topics such as AI, quantum computing and cosmology – all of which are quite daunting! We persevere and continue to try to understand topics like these that are very challenging. We look up terms and concepts we don’t understand and then teach each other. We also love to read articles on climate change and medical science, as these feel more relatable. We plan to get the recordings of the talks from October’s New Scientist Live , so we can watch together and discuss. We want to thank you for making science accessible to us – we all feel that it’s important as we get older to not give in to the temptation to ignore all the new discoveries and changes in the world. Diana Currie, Dawn Segrue and the Marlow Science Group An article about Benjamin Libet’s experiments in the 1980s showing there was a time gap between the brain making a decision and conscious awareness of that decision inspired me, as a psychotherapist, to find a way of using that gap in the field of psychological therapy. Two years of exploration and testing later, I taught the first cohort of students, and now it is being employed by psychologists, counsellors, psychiatrists and psychotherapists all over the world. Terence Watts 4 of the most memorable biotech moments in modern scientific history On the eve of New Scientist’s 70th anniversary, newsroom legend Andy Coghlan reveals four of the most dramatic and surprising moments from his storied career Back in 2019, I stumbled across an eye-catching magazine on the shelves of a Tesco store. The title-page article caught my eye: “Does this one microbe cause all these conditions… and does that mean we can beat them?” It was at that moment that I truly fell in love with biology. Years have passed, and I have since graduated with a science degree from the University of Edinburgh and am now a returning student at my alma mater pursuing a master of research postgraduate degree in life sciences. One day, I aim to be able to contribute – even if just a little – to aiding humanity in its endless fight against malady and illness. All of my academic achievements thus far may very well not have been possible had it not been for that magazine that caught my eye, that day in August 2019. And for that, I quite literally owe New Scientist all my academic achievements, and all that I have done, to this day. Stephen Wang I am 87 and have been reading New Scientist every week since October 1964. I still have a note from my grandson, Maximilian, from when he was 5 years old, thanking me for reading New Scientist with him. He is now studying biology at my one-time college, Merton, at the University of Oxford. In the meantime, he has already succeeded, while travelling with his mother in Amazonia, in identifying, describing, naming and publishing a new genus and species of damselfly. He and I continue to discuss issues like evolution together, though I am a classicist by training. Anthony J. Nieduszynski Your magazine is vital to our family. It sparks many conversations at the kitchen table. Our 11-year-old grandson keeps beating us to the latest issue. Our 6-year-old grandson has been enthralled with the cover art since he was 3. I cut out the cartoons and post them on the fridge. They have become the “cartoon of the week”. Often my grandsons see details I didn’t even catch. Krystyna Rodriguez The 12 strangest science stories we can’t stop thinking about From subconscious finger sniffing to rats driving cars, New Scientist staff have reported on many weird, wild or utterly bonkers discoveries and inventions in the 70 years since we began I have been a reader for almost all the publication’s life, as I first starte

item.title: Portugal did the extraordinary with Cristiano Ronaldo. Can they do it without him?
item.description: The captain, the talisman, the brand: former teammates and experts discuss Portugal entering a new era after 23 years There are days football fans hope will never come. For Portugal, this is one of them. For 23 years, Cristiano Ronaldo has been more than the country’s greatest footballer; he has been its defining sporting figure, a symbol of national pride and constant presence in the lives of supporters. After 234 appearances and 146 goals, the No 7 brought that chapter to a close and on Saturday night the team will play their first game without him . The national side are losing more than a great footballer; they are also losing one of the world’s biggest brands. Daniel Sá, the executive director of the Portuguese institute of marketing administration, believes Portugal require reinvention to attract at least some of the millions of viewers who tuned in because of CR7. Continue reading...

item.dc:creator: Our Reporters
item.content:encoded: Going by the number of women that have emerged candidates in the last primary elections of all the political parties in Nigeria, next year’s general polls is bound to witness fewer number of women contesting elective positions. Weekend Trust reports that while more women indicated interests in contesting by obtaining forms to secure the tickets of their parties, most of them could not go beyond the preliminary stages, with many of them either withdrawing, not considered in the consensus arrangements, or defeated in the early stages. Checks by our correspondents revealed that a higher number of women had indicated interests in contesting for state assembly seats, but the number dwindled for those going for House of Representatives seats, again, dropping drastically for Senate and getting terribly low on governorship. When the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) released the names of the presidential candidates for 2027, only two out of the 18 candidates, which constitutes 11.1per cent of the total candidates, are women, despite making up 49.32 per cent of Nigeria’s population. Amidst campaigns, Borno, Niger children remain in captivity Tinubu booed at Abuja mosque after Friday prayers They are up against 15 men, including President Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress (APC), former Vice President Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), and other candidates across the political parties. The two women are Ada Elizabeth Okwori of the National Democratic Party (NDP) and Esther Iken Okereke of the National Rescue Movement (NRM). Also, there are four female vice presidential candidates who will be contesting. These are Hajiya Bintu Konto (LP), Ofordile Peace Egobia (APP), Nafisat Usaku (DLA) and Patience Key (YPP) INEC figures obtained by Weekend Trust, showed that 469 women are among the 4,863 candidates listed for the Senate and House of Representatives elections, while only two of the 18 presidential candidates are women. The figures indicate that fewer than one in every 10 candidates contesting the National Assembly elections is female, while women constitute just over one in every 10 presidential candidates. The Senate has the lowest female representation, with 123 women among 1,303 candidates, representing 9.4 per cent. The House of Representatives has 346 female candidates out of 3,560, representing 9.7 per cent. The figures were calculated from the party and gender fields contained in INEC’s final list of candidates. The figures reflect a pattern in Nigerian politics in which women participate extensively in elections but remain largely absent from the institutions where political decisions are made. Data from 2015 show that only one woman contested the presidency, while four women were listed as vice presidential candidates, with 14 political parties participating. By 2019, female participation had increased, with five women contesting the presidency and 23 contesting the vice presidency, as the number of political parties also rose to 72. In the 2023 election, only one woman contested for the presidency, while no woman contested for the vice presidency. The number of participating political parties also dropped to 18. Since the return to democratic rule in 1999, there has been underrepresentation of women in the parliament. For instance, in the 10th National Assembly, women account for only about 3.7 per cent of senators and 4.4 per cent of members of the House of Representatives. Fourteen state assemblies do not have a single woman. The states are Kaduna, Kebbi, Sokoto, Zamfara, Jigawa, Kano, Bauchi, Gombe, Yobe and Plateau. Political analysts and civil society organisations have observed that since the return of democracy in 1999, the number of women who have contested and won elective positions has been disproportionately low compared to men. In the current Senate, out of 109 senators, only four – Ireti kingibe, Natasha Akpoti-Uduaghan, Ipalibo Banigo and Idiat Oluranti Adebule are women, leaving the Red Chamber of the National Assembly to be dominated by men, while in the Green Chamber, only 17 women are currently serving out of the 360 total members, representing only 4.7 per cent of the legislative seats. As issues relating to primaries are about to be concluded, the development has again raised the question about why the number of women participating in politics is shrinking despite the encouragement, enlightenment and examples in other climes, which should have served to encourage Nigerian women. Analysts say development across the globe should have spurred more women in Nigeria to go into politics. Currently, the president of Tanzania, Samia Suluhu Hassan and that of Namibia, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, are women. Weekend Trust recalls how, in the past, the low number of women participating in politics became an issue of concern that deliberate efforts were made to encourage their participation through sensitisation and lowering the financial cost, with many political parties offering their nomination forms to women at no cost. Concerned groups and individuals have attributed the dwindling number to factors that include cost of participation, cultural and religious restrictions, as well as the perception about women in politics A coalition of women-led movements and civil society organisations recently raised concerns over the declining participation of women in Nigeria’s electoral process, warning that the 2027 general elections could produce even fewer female lawmakers than the 2023 polls, unless urgent reforms are implemented. Presenting the findings of an audit conducted on the primaries, the Executive Director of Invictus Africa, Bukky Shonibare, revealed that women’s participation remained critically low across most political parties. According to the audit, only three of the 22 political parties recorded female aspirant participation above 20 per cent, with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) recording 28.2 per cent female participation, followed by the Young Progressives Party (YPP) with 22.2 per cent and the Young Progressives Party (YP) with 20 per cent. The National Rescue Movement (NRM) recorded 11.8 per cent female participation, while the All Progressives Congress (APC) had 10.4 per cent, and the New Nigeria People’s Party (NNPP) recorded no female aspirant. The audit also found that only three women emerged as senatorial candidates across all parties, prompting fears that women could occupy just 2.7 per cent of Senate seats after the 2027 elections if current trends persist. Shonibare identified several barriers confronting female aspirants, including forced withdrawals, opaque consensus arrangements and last-minute candidate substitutions. A co-founder and Executive Director of the Voice of Women Empowerment Foundation, Toun Okewale Sonaiya, on her part, warned that unless corrective measures were taken, women’s political representation in 2027 could be worse than what was recorded in the 2023 elections. Another woman, Aisha Abdullahi Hudu, the chief executive officer and founder of United Women for Peace Initiative, said point blank that the men were not carrying the women along. She said: “They don’t want women to occupy one seat to the other.” Reserved Seat bill for women Our correspondent reports that there’s a Reserved Seat bill contained in the constitutional amendment legislation seeking to create additional elective seats exclusively for women in the Senate, House of Representatives and State Houses of Assembly. It seeks to create additional constitutionally recognised seats strictly for women. In the Senate, each state and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) would have one extra seat reserved exclusively for women. Also, the House of Representatives will have one extra seat for each state and the FCT. At the state level, each House of Assembly would add three women-only seats. But the bill

item.title: World Diabetes Day: High cost pushes drugs, special diets out of reach
item.description: As the world marks the 2026 World Diabetes Day today, attention is once again drawn to the importance of early diagnosis, timely treatment and sustained care in preventing complications and saving lives. But for many Nigerians living with the condition, the challenge goes beyond early detection to affording medication, special diets and regular medical checks needed to manage the disease. Some patients who spoke to Weekend Trust said the rising cost of treatment had pushed them into financial hardship, forcing them to ration prescribed drugs, compromise their diets or go for days without medication. For Mrs Ngunengen Akpam, living with diabetes has become a daily struggle, not only against the disease but also against the rising cost of managing it. Tinubu booed at Abuja mosque after Friday prayers Women and race to 2027 The burden is compounded by her responsibility to also support her diabetic mother, Mama Lydia Acka, making the cost of medication, food and routine medical care a constant source of worry for the family. Akpam told one of our correspondents that the prices of essential diabetes medications had increased considerably over the years, making it increasingly difficult to maintain the treatment prescribed by her doctors. She recalled that Metformin, one of the drugs she takes, which sold for N700 for a pack of three cards in 2015, now costs about N2,500. Similarly, Dormin, which previously sold for N700, now costs N3,500 for a pack of 10 cards, she said. “The cost of drugs has increased tremendously. I take my medication twice daily, so it is not easy. In a month, we spend so much, especially when you have another diabetic person to cater for,” she said. Medication, however, is only part of the financial burden. Akpam explained that managing diabetes also requires adherence to a carefully regulated diet, including millet, beans and vegetables, which have also become expensive. Although the price of millet had dropped from more than N1,200 to N600 per mudu during the harvest season, she said her financial circumstances still made it difficult to consistently afford the recommended food items. The experience is similar for Mrs Elahi Onu, who has lived with diabetes for 11 years and whose treatment has become a major financial responsibility for her children. Onu said her children spend at least N25,000 monthly on medication alone, while more than N60,000 goes into providing the special diet recommended for managing her condition. She listed unripe plantain, beans, vegetables, basmati rice and grains such as millet among the food items she had been advised to eat. “These special types of food are costly and drain the pockets of my children. “Sometimes there is a delay in supplies of these items to me. I will be forced to go hungry for the period or fall back to any available food,” she said. item.content:encoded: As the world marks the 2026 World Diabetes Day today, attention is once again drawn to the importance of early diagnosis, timely treatment and sustained care in preventing complications and saving lives. But for many Nigerians living with the condition, the challenge goes beyond early detection to affording medication, special diets and regular medical checks needed to manage the disease. Some patients who spoke to Weekend Trust said the rising cost of treatment had pushed them into financial hardship, forcing them to ration prescribed drugs, compromise their diets or go for days without medication. For Mrs Ngunengen Akpam, living with diabetes has become a daily struggle, not only against the disease but also against the rising cost of managing it. Tinubu booed at Abuja mosque after Friday prayers Women and race to 2027 The burden is compounded by her responsibility to also support her diabetic mother, Mama Lydia Acka, making the cost of medication, food and routine medical care a constant source of worry for the family. Akpam told one of our correspondents that the prices of essential diabetes medications had increased considerably over the years, making it increasingly difficult to maintain the treatment prescribed by her doctors. She recalled that Metformin, one of the drugs she takes, which sold for N700 for a pack of three cards in 2015, now costs about N2,500. Similarly, Dormin, which previously sold for N700, now costs N3,500 for a pack of 10 cards, she said. “The cost of drugs has increased tremendously. I take my medication twice daily, so it is not easy. In a month, we spend so much, especially when you have another diabetic person to cater for,” she said. Medication, however, is only part of the financial burden. Akpam explained that managing diabetes also requires adherence to a carefully regulated diet, including millet, beans and vegetables, which have also become expensive. Although the price of millet had dropped from more than N1,200 to N600 per mudu during the harvest season, she said her financial circumstances still made it difficult to consistently afford the recommended food items. The experience is similar for Mrs Elahi Onu, who has lived with diabetes for 11 years and whose treatment has become a major financial responsibility for her children. Onu said her children spend at least N25,000 monthly on medication alone, while more than N60,000 goes into providing the special diet recommended for managing her condition. She listed unripe plantain, beans, vegetables, basmati rice and grains such as millet among the food items she had been advised to eat. “These special types of food are costly and drain the pockets of my children. “Sometimes there is a delay in supplies of these items to me. I will be forced to go hungry for the period or fall back to any available food,” she said. Beyond feeding and medication, Onu said she also had to contend with the cost of routine medical examinations. She disclosed that one of her prescribed medications, Triviamet, costs about N13,000 for a pack of 35 tablets, apart from the other drugs she requires. The additional expenses have continued to stretch the finances of a family already spending tens of thousands of naira monthly on her treatment and feeding. Onu called on the government to intervene through reduced drug prices, subsidies and improved access to treatment, warning that people living with diabetes should not be left struggling to afford basic necessities for managing the condition. She also stressed the need for early intervention and sustained support for patients, particularly as the world marks the 2026 World Diabetes Day under the theme, “Early Action on Diabetes”. Living with diabetes without regular treatment For Mark Tongir, who has lived with diabetes for 29 years, prevailing economic realities have made managing the condition increasingly difficult. Tongir said he spends about N14,000 weekly on medication, but financial constraints sometimes force him to buy the drugs in small quantities rather than purchase a complete pack. He said the situation had become particularly challenging amid the prevailing economic hardship, which had affected his ability to meet his treatment needs consistently. “I wish the government would subsidise the treatment,” he said. Another patient, Ahubi Anebi, who was diagnosed with diabetes more than 15 years ago, said financial difficulties had sometimes forced her to go for several days without medication. Anebi said her health had deteriorated to the extent that she could no longer engage in paid employment to raise money for her treatment. She explained that she previously earned a living by preparing and selling fast food by the roadside, but her inability to continue the business had left her dependent on relatives and other well-wishers. “I hardly could adhere to the prescribed diet because the money to buy it is not available. I’m just living by the grace of God. “Since I could no longer cook fast food by the roadside through which I could earn money to buy my food or drugs, I sometimes go for days without taking any, except when relatives dash me some money,” she said. Without a regular source of income, Anebi depends on occasional financial assistance to obtain medication and food. She and other patients appealed to the government to introduce measures that would make diabetes treatment affordable, particularly for low-income earners, elderly people and those who depend on relatives for survival. They called for subsidised medication, affordable healthcare services and improved access to treatment to prevent complications associated with irregular medication and poor disease management. An NGO offering free blood sugar test ‘15m persons living with diabetes for less than 200 specialists’ Meanwhile, the Endocrine and Metabolism Society of Nigeria (EMSON) has estimated that diabetes affects between six and seven per cent of Nigerians, representing approximately 15 million people. Its president, Prof. Andrew Uloko, warned that many Nigerians were living with diabetes without knowing their status, while those already diagnosed faced difficulties accessing essential medicines, glucose-monitoring equipment, laboratory investigations and specialist care. He identified population growth, ageing, urbanisation, changing dietary habits and physical inactivity as factors reshaping Nigeria’s endocrine disease landscape. Prof. Anas Sabir, an endocrinologist, also estimated that between 10 and 15 million Nigerians were living with diabetes. Sabir put the prevalence of the disease at between 5.7 and seven per cent, identifying late presentation and high treatment costs as major challenges. “Most patients pay out of pocket. Even the NHIA does not give coverage of everything and, even when it does, it is not very effective,” he said. Sabir said patients could present with diabetes alongside hypertension, dyslipidaemia and obesity, further complicating Nigeria’s disease burden. He added that Nigeria had fewer than 200 practising endocrinologists, with specialist training concentrated mainly in tertiary hospitals in Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt and Kano. Africans living with diabetes may hit 59.5m – WHO Similarly, the World Health Organisation (WHO) has raised concerns about the growing burden of diabetes across Africa, warning that millions of people remain undiagnosed until serious complications develop. In his World Diabetes Day 2026 message, WHO Regional Director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, said an estimated 24.6 million adults aged between 20 and 79 were living with diabetes in the African Region in 2024. He warned that the figure was projected to rise to 59.5 million by 2050 if urgent interventions were not sustained. More concerning, Janabi said nearly three out of every four adults living with diabetes in the region remained undiagnosed, representing the highest proportion globally. According to h

item.title: Amidst campaigns, Borno, Niger children remain in captivity
item.description: As the campaign season hots up, families of the abducted children in Borno and Niger states are still looking up to the authorities for intervention. Weekend Trust reports that while the pupils kidnapped in Borno have spent 213 days in captivity, students abducted in Niger have also remained in the hands of their captors for more than two weeks. Today makes it 213 days of agony and sleepless nights for the families of the abducted children in Mussa and Lassa communities of Askira-Uba Local Government Area in Borno State. The78 children, including toddlers less than two years old, who were abducted following two separate operations by bandits and insurgents, are still in captivity, even as politicians intensify campaigns for political power. The nightmare began on May 15, 2026 when at least 42 pupils and students were taken from their classrooms in Mussa Primary and Secondary School. Weeks later, on June 29, another set of 36 students were abducted in Government Day Secondary School, Lassa, further escalating security concerns in the area. Women and race to 2027 How IDPs built Abuja’s largest beans market Since then, the whereabouts of the children have remained unknown, plunging the families into a state of painful trauma. The Mussa school children were abducted on the same day as the 44 pupils and teachers from a school in the Oriire Local Government Area of Oyo State. But unlike the Mussa schoolchildren that have remained in captivity, the Oyo children were rescued on July 10, 2026 after 56 days in captivity after President Bola Ahmed Tinubu gave marching orders to heads of security operatives to rescue them. Weekend Trust reports that parents of the abducted pupils in Borno have on various occasions expressed frustration over what they described as “silence” from both the federal and state governments. The families are alleging that the authorities have entirely abandoned them; expressing fear that their children may have been forgotten by the same people they voted to power to protect them. The chairman of the parents of the abducted children, Mr Ishaku Suya, told our correspondent that the communities had remained in despair since the abduction of the schoolchildren. “Officially, I have not heard anything from the federal or state governments. Nobody is saying anything. And nobody has reached out to us from the side of the abductors,” he said.
